title: Visiting another stream
hookLine: all are welcome at any gurdwara; courtesy is enough

lines: SHOES OFF, HEAD COVERED, HANDS WASHED.
cards: A shoe rack by the door, already full. A basket of orange and blue head scarves for anyone who came without one. A small trough of water for washing hands.
Nobody at the entrance asks which stream you belong to, or whether you're a Sikh at all. Someone may smile and point you toward the scarves. That's the whole admission process.
This week has been full of questions Sikhs disagree about. It ends at the door every stream keeps open.

teach.b: Look back at the week: open questions held kindly, the meat question and its different plates, the Dasam Granth and its shared devotion, women among the five and a conversation that continues, many voices, and one Granth at the front of every room.
What makes all that livable is this: any Sikh, and anyone else, can walk into a gurdwara of a stream not their own and be welcome.
What's asked is courtesy, not agreement. Cover your head. Take off your shoes.
Leave tobacco and alcohol outside. Sit on the floor with everyone else, facing the Granth, and don't turn your back to it or point your feet at it.
If karah prashad, the warm sweet offering, is handed out, receive it in cupped hands. If you're invited to langar, sit in the row and eat what's served. No one checks your theology at the door.
Gurbani gives a line for this openness.
On Ang 671, Guru Arjan says, here in paraphrase, I have made everyone my friend, and I am a friend to all.

A Nihang gurdwara may feel different from a Western sangat's, and a Namdhari gathering different again: the dress, the tunes, the pace. A visitor doesn't need to settle any of this week's questions to sit down.
Courtesy is enough. Welcome does the rest.

how: Gurdwaras of every Sikh stream welcome visitors of any background; guests cover their heads, remove their shoes, leave tobacco and alcohol outside, sit on the floor facing the Guru Granth Sahib, receive karah prashad in cupped hands and may share langar.

o: any gurdwara welcomes you; courtesy is all it asks
only Sikhs of the same group may enter
a guest must agree with that gurdwara's views

games.q: inside visiting another stream: tap the pairs.
p: covered with a scarf or turban

s: you must belong to a gurdwara's stream to enter it
anyone is welcome. courtesy is asked, not agreement.
visitors are asked not to point their feet at the Granth
sit on the floor facing it, and don't turn your back to it.
you need to settle the week's open questions before visiting
no one checks your theology at the door.

games.q: you're visiting a gurdwara of a stream you've never seen, and someone hands you karah prashad. what do you do?
o: decline it politely because you're not a member.
ask what stream they belong to first.
games.why: cupped hands is the custom. no membership, no questions: courtesy is enough.

practice: Picture a gurdwara you've never been to, or any place of worship you've wondered about, and walk through the visit in your mind: the shoes, the head covering, washing your hands, sitting down on the carpet.
Notice any nervousness and let it out with the breath; if you pray, ask for an open heart on the way.

wordCard.voice: Visiting another stream. Anyone is welcome at any gurdwara; what's asked is a covered head, bare feet, and courtesy, not agreement. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: the Sikh place of worship.

carryVoice: Your line: courtesy is enough. A covered head and bare feet, and you're in. Rest well.
